body.heading: The sunflower's arithmetic
paragraphs: Look at the face of a sunflower and you will see seeds arranged in spirals — some curving clockwise, some anti-clockwise. Count them and the two numbers are very often neighbours in the Fibonacci sequence: 34 and 55, or 55 and 89. Pinecones and pineapples play the same game with smaller numbers, like 8 and 13.

This is not decoration. Packing each new seed at a fixed angle (about 137.5 degrees, the “golden angle”) fills the head with no gaps and no wasted space. The Fibonacci counts are what that angle naturally produces — arithmetic growing in a flowerbed.

body.heading: Hexagons and snowflakes
paragraphs: Bees build honeycomb from hexagons, the most economical tiling shape, while snowflakes grow with six-fold symmetry because of the way water molecules bond as they freeze. Each snowflake's six arms experience the same air at the same moments, so they grow in near-perfect matching — symmetry written by physics, not by an artist.

Zebra stripes, leopard spots and the ripples on a sand dune are patterns too, made by growth and chemistry rather than by rulers. The deep lesson of natural patterns: simple rules, repeated faithfully, generate endless variety.

body.heading: Try it: a pattern safari
paragraphs: Go on a pattern safari with a camera or sketchbook: find a spiral, a hexagon, a branching pattern (trees, rivers, lightning-shaped cracks), and stripes or spots. For each one, guess the simple rule that might have grown it.
Finish with the sunflower test: find a pinecone and count its spirals in both directions. If you land on 5 and 8, or 8 and 13, you have caught mathematics in the wild.

takeaway: Nature builds by simple rules repeated faithfully — count a sunflower's spirals and you will find a number sequence staring back.
